action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active and chronic denervation in the cervical and lumbosacral regions with thoracic paraspinal fibrillations and tongue fasciculations; normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No structural, vascular, demyelinating or neoplastic brain or brainstem lesion; subtle symmetric corticospinal tract T2 signal only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cord compression or cord signal change; old L5-S1 surgical changes without recurrent herniation or root compression.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 892 U/L (5.1x ULN) and blood lead 24 mcg/dL; blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: here the occupational lead exposure justifies a repeat blood lead level.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 82% predicted and SNIP 74 cmH2O, within normal limits: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude ALS.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide do not interact with riluzole; light alcohol use only; baseline and scheduled transaminase monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it; his alcohol intake is light.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
Do not attribute the motor syndrome to lead or treat it with chelation: a blood lead of 24-28 mcg/dL does not cause upper motor neuron signs or multi-region anterior horn cell denervation.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive left upper limb-onset weakness with upper motor neuron signs (bilateral Hoffman signs, brisk reflexes in all limbs and a left Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar (tongue atrophy and fasciculations), cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall. His CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnoea can mask nocturnal hypoventilation, so review CPAP use and sleep symptoms at each visit.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

Refer to occupational health to stop further lead exposure and follow the blood lead level (24 mcg/dL, previously 28 mcg/dL) until it falls; the lead level does not explain the upper and lower motor neuron syndrome.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

differential.key_features: supports: occupational lead exposure, blood lead 28 then 24 mcg/dL; against: lead does not cause upper motor neuron signs (Hoffman, Babinski), and EMG shows multi-region anterior horn cell denervation including thoracic paraspinals and tongue fasciculations with normal sensory studies and no conduction slowing or block, which lead neuropathy does not produce
supports: asymmetric arm-predominant lower motor neuron weakness; against: upper motor neuron signs, normal motor conduction velocities and no conduction block, bulbar involvement

differential.diagnosis: Hereditary motor neuropathy / CMT2 motor variant
differential.key_features: against: adult onset with progression over 9 months, no family history and upper motor neuron signs
supports: CK 892 U/L; against: fasciculations, neurogenic EMG with fibrillations and large MUPs, upper motor neuron signs, no finger flexor or quadriceps-predominant pattern

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: bilateral Hoffman signs, brisk reflexes and a left Babinski sign with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on EMG and the bulbar region clinically (tongue atrophy and fasciculations), with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.

CK 892 U/L is 5.1x ULN, higher than usual in ALS: consider a myopathic contributor clinically, while the neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs argues against a primary myopathy.

FVC 82% predicted and SNIP 74 cmH2O are normal at baseline. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

A blood lead of 24-28 mcg/dL needs occupational exposure control, but lead does not cause upper motor neuron signs and lead neuropathy does not produce multi-region anterior horn cell denervation with normal sensory studies.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The exposure is real and needs occupational follow-up (repeat blood lead 24 mcg/dL), but lead does not cause upper motor neuron signs, and the EMG shows multi-region anterior horn cell denervation, including thoracic paraspinals and tongue fasciculations, with normal sensory studies and no conduction slowing or block, which lead neuropathy does not produce.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. D is a 59-year-old active duty firefighter who presents with a 9-month history of progressive left arm weakness and visible wasting. He first noticed difficulty performing overhead activities at work and reduced grip strength in his left hand approximately 9 months ago. He was placed on light duty 3 months ago when his supervising officer noted visible wasting of his left forearm and hand.

He initially attributed the weakness to a shoulder injury sustained during a training exercise 11 months ago and received physical therapy for 2 months without improvement. He has visible twitching in his left arm and both calves that his wife describes as involuntary and constant. He has developed cramps in his left hand and bilateral calves.

Over the past 4 months, he has noticed milder right arm weakness and bilateral leg weakness, particularly when climbing stairs or pulling heavy equipment. He denies sensory symptoms. He has no swallowing difficulties. No bladder or bowel changes.

He is concerned about his ability to continue working. His occupational health physician noted that he may have had heavy metal exposures (lead, mercury) during firefighting activities and ordered a heavy metals panel. This returned elevated lead level at 28 mcg/dL (normal <5 mcg/dL), raising the question of lead toxicity as an etiology of his weakness. He was referred to neurology for comprehensive evaluation.
